content: The implementation of nutrition interventions globally is supported by sharing programmatic details, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. This approach provides concrete examples of how guidelines are translated into actionable strategies. The Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA), launched in November 2012, has become an essential resource for tracking the implementation of various nutrition policies and interventions. Its usage has steadily increased, emphasizing the importance of a robust system for routinely collecting relevant data, including health determinants, therapeutic adherence, and program performance metrics. Such data collection ensures the effectiveness and sustainability of micronutrient distribution programs, ultimately contributing to the realization of the right to health for all population groups. Monitoring disparities in accessibility, availability, acceptability, and quality of interventions across different groups is crucial for designing improved public health programs. Indicators for monitoring can be informed by the social determinants of health framework, enabling the identification and resolution of inequities. The design of sound implementation strategies, such as those outlined in the WHO guideline on the use of multiple micronutrient powders for point-of-use fortification of foods for infants and children aged 6–23 months and 2–12 years, serves as a foundation for scaling up efforts. Effective monitoring requires the collection and organization of suitable data, and ethical considerations for monitoring systems are outlined in previous sections. The development of this guideline adhered to WHO's evidence-informed guideline development procedures, as detailed in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development, established in 2009, oversees the process, with representatives from various WHO departments involved in providing scientific nutrition advice. The guideline development group, active during 2013–2014, included experts from diverse disciplines and WHO regions, ensuring a balanced representation. Efforts were made to include content experts, methodologists, health professionals, and technical staff from ministries of health, while excluding representatives from commercial organizations. The names and biographies of group members were made publicly available for transparency. An external group of resource experts assisted in evidence assessment, research prioritization, and program considerations but did not participate in the final formulation of recommendations. The guideline underwent peer review by eight experts, who provided technical feedback on the final draft. Peer reviewers were tasked with identifying errors, clarifying content, and addressing implementation considerations, but they did not alter the recommendations formulated by the guideline development group. The scope of the guideline was defined through an initial set of questions, drafted using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes) format. These questions were reviewed and refined by the WHO Steering Committee and the guideline development group. Meetings held in 2013 and 2014 in Geneva and Cancun allowed the group to discuss programmatic experiences, review systematic evidence, and finalize recommendations. Systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles were used to appraise the quality of evidence, considering factors such as study design, consistency, directness, and precision. Decision-making procedures were established at the outset of meetings, with members voting on the direction and strength of recommendations. If unanimous consensus was not achieved, further deliberations and a second round of voting were conducted. A two-thirds majority was required for approval if consensus remained elusive. Divergent opinions were documented, and voting results were retained by WHO for five years. WHO staff and external experts involved in evidence collection did not participate in decision-making. Conflict-of-interest management followed WHO's strict guidelines. All participants submitted declarations of interest and verbally disclosed potential conflicts at the start of meetings. Interests that could reasonably affect the expert's objectivity were scrutinized to ensure the integrity of the guideline development process.
